summary: The IRS Whistleblower Office has published an annual report to Congress for every fiscal year since its first report (June 2008, with informant-claim figures for FY2003-FY2007), up to FY2024. All 18 are stored and their numbers recorded: claims received, closures by reason, open inventory, awards paid (count, amount, and the 7623(a)/(b) split where published), collections, processing times, and sequestration cuts. Definitions change often (potential-7623(b) submissions, then claims by year of receipt, then claims built), and prior years are revised in each report, so each report is a separate row. Law (26 USC 7623, 26 CFR 301.7623-1/-2/-4), TIGTA 2023, three GAO reports (product pages only), a Tax Court opinion and the $104 million Birkenfeld award (confirmed by the IRS FY2012 report under a privacy waiver; name from press) complete the picture.

cases.summary: IRS paid a whistleblower award of US$104 million; the whistleblower gave a limited privacy waiver so the IRS could confirm the payment. Widely reported as Bradley Birkenfeld, the former UBS banker whose information exposed UBS secret Swiss accounts held by US taxpayers; the IRS report itself does not name him or the target.
cases.quote: One claim paid in FY 2012 was accompanied by a limited privacy waiver that permits the IRS to confirm that, on August 27, 2012, the IRS paid an award of $104 million to a whistleblower.
cases.notes: award_amount scale: million. Name and target (UBS) not in the IRS document; see the reported row for the identification.

cases.summary: A husband and wife reported a taxpayer (a firm that later pleaded guilty to conspiracy) and were rejected as untimely; the Tax Court reversed in 2015, the parties agreed a 24% award, and in 2016 the Court held that the criminal fine and civil forfeitures, not just tax restitution, count as collected proceeds.
cases.quote: parties subsequently agreed that Ps are eligible for an award of 24% ... The targeted taxpayer pleaded guilty to a violation of 18 U.S.C. sec. 371 and paid $74,131,694 in tax restitution, a criminal fine, and
cases.notes: Stipulated split (p. 5): tax restitution $20,000,001; criminal fine $22,050,000; civil forfeiture $15,821,000; relinquished forfeited funds $16,260,693. Award amount not stated in the opinion; media reported $17.8 million (see leads). Target unnamed in the opinion.

cases.summary: Whistleblower 22716-13W v. Commissioner (146 T.C.): the information led to a small tax restitution and FBAR civil penalties over $2 million; the IRS denied the claim, saying FBAR penalties do not count toward the $2 million threshold.

cases.summary: Former UBS banker Bradley Birkenfeld, who exposed UBS help for US clients hiding money in Swiss accounts (and served prison time for helping a client evade tax), announced through his lawyer that the IRS awarded him US$104 million.

cases.notes: Amounts in USD million. Birkenfeld went public himself. The IRS FY2012 report confirms a $104 million payment on 27 Aug 2012 under a privacy waiver (case irs-2012-08-27-104m). events.title: Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 creates section 7623(b)
events.description: Section 406 of the Act (PL 109-432) re-designates the old discretionary informant-reward law as 7623(a) and adds mandatory awards of 15-30% for cases over $2 million, a Whistleblower Office and Tax Court appeals. Applies to information provided after 19 December 2006.

events.quote: For information provided to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) after December 19, 2006, new section 7623(b) generally requires the IRS to pay awards

events.title: Original informant-reward law
events.description: The authority now in section 7623(a) originates in an 1867 law allowing the Treasury to pay sums for detecting and punishing tax violators.

events.quote: The 1996 amendments also changed the source of funds from IRS operating funds to proceeds of amounts collected from the taxpayer (other than interest).

events.description: From July 2009 the IRS waits until the taxpayer can no longer claim a refund (generally two years after the last payment) before paying an award, delaying some payments to FY2010-2011.

events.description: Revised Internal Revenue Manual sets procedures for intake and award determinations, including letting 7623(b) whistleblowers comment on preliminary awards; 7623(a) claims filed from 1 July 2010 use the same percentages as 7623(b).
events.quote: awards paid in section 7623(a) cases submitted on or after July 1, 2010 ... will be determined using the same criteria and percentages that apply to 7623(b) claims.

events.description: The IRS proposes defining collected proceeds for 7623(a) and (b), including reductions of overpayment credit balances and refund-prevention claims.

programs.name: IRS Whistleblower Program (Whistleblower Office), 26 U.S.C. § 7623
programs.notes: Section 7623(b) (Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006, § 406) makes awards of 15-30% of proceeds mandatory when proceeds in dispute exceed $2 million (and, for individuals, gross income over $200,000); appealable to the Tax Court. Smaller cases fall under the discretionary section 7623(a), whose roots go back to an 1867 informant-reward law; before 2006 the IRS ran it as the Informant Claims Program (awards of 1%, 10% or 15%, generally capped at $10 million, under Policy Statement P-4-27). This file keeps the pre-2006 informant-reward figures (FY2003-FY2007) under the same program_id because the legal authority (now 7623(a)) is continuous; split it out (e.g. usa-irs-informant) if preferred. Whistleblower Office set up in early 2007 (first director appointed 2 Feb 2007). Since 2018 proceeds include criminal fines, forfeitures and reporting-requirement (FBAR-type) penalties; since 2019 the Taxpayer First Act adds status notices and anti-retaliation protection (7623(d)). Award payments are subject to sequestration (5.7-8.7% a year since March 2013).
